editorial.headline: Technical Testing, With a Clear Bali Route for Foreign Capital
editorial.standfirst: A bounded technical-testing activity open at every listed scale, with full foreign ownership nationally and no Bali moratorium block.
editorial.body:
This activity is a deliberately bounded home for technical testing and analysis. It covers work that is neither certification, inspection, verification nor validation, and that is not otherwise placed in a separately classified technical-testing activity. “Other” does not mean unlimited: the record sets clear edges around the category. Testing involving ionising radiation, the organisation of interlaboratory proficiency testing, and the development of technical standards used as testing references all sit outside it. Laboratory security-and-order operation is also outside the scope when it is separate from the testing activity itself.

The activity is available at every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That is broad access, but it does not dilute the definition. The relevant business is one undertaking the specified technical testing and analysis; the registration should follow the work actually performed rather than absorb adjacent functions that the record distinguishes. For founders, the useful reading is precise rather than expansive: start with the nature of the technical testing or analysis, then keep it within the stated boundary.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is direct. The activity is marked TERBUKA and has a maximum foreign ownership of 100% under Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In plain English, the national record imposes no foreign-share ceiling below full ownership for this activity. That conclusion applies to this defined technical-testing and analysis activity, at the scales named in the record. It is a clear opening, not an invitation to treat every laboratory-adjacent undertaking as the same registered activity.

Bali does not reverse that national opening. Its Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the record states that, at the Besar scale, the OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi. For that reason, this activity is not blocked by Bali’s permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium. A foreign-owned business can therefore register this activity in Bali today: the record marks no Bali block. The risk description is central to the conclusion, not a hidden caveat; the higher-risk position stated for the Besar scale is why the moratorium does not close this route.
